name: Dana Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won’t be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work days on a general surgery ward at St Aldric's, the regional hospital, which is a 40-minute drive from our village. Shift starts at quarter past seven, so I'm on the road by half six. Most of my patients are a day or two after an operation: gallbladders, hernias, the odd bowel resection. It's drains, wound dressings, pain scores, getting people up and walking, and a lot of phone calls chasing the surgeons for discharge decisions.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love wounds, which sounds strange. Seeing a messy one close up properly over a week because you got the dressing right is really satisfying. What wears me out is the drive, the petrol and the car loan, and the fact that I'm on lower pay than the nurses at the city hospitals. My girlfriend Ines is a teaching assistant at the village primary school, so neither of us is exactly rolling in it. We've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank at any time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out as it's written. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Okay, I can picture that pretty easily, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm relieved, and that the money should go into staff now instead of shiny software. I'd share something on social media about how we needed more nurses, not more apps. That's been my line for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changing sounds lovely until you remember that nothing changing means the car loan, the 40-minute drive and the same short-staffed shifts. My job is safe, it's the money that's tight. I'd still be checking the bank app before I fill the tank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, honestly. I'd try to set up a standing order of 40 a month into a savings pot so we're not one car repair from disaster. I might use the AI helper on my phone now and then to plan revision for the wound care course I keep meaning to apply for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit flat, because the things that actually bother me don't change either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the car repair that would tip you over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter it was the clutch, 600, and we had to borrow from Ines's mum. That was embarrassing. If something like that happened again we'd be on the credit card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said "nothing changing sounds lovely". Who would you be glad about, at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The healthcare assistants, mostly, and our ward clerk Rosa, who does all the bed booking. If AI really did nothing much, Rosa keeps her job and I keep my sanity, because she knows every bed in the building.

say: I'd say I'm **relieved** and the money should go on staff, not software.
I'd post that the health service needs **more nurses**, not more apps.
think: My **job** is safe; the **money** is what stays tight.
The **car loan** and the long commute still eat my pay every month.
do: Keep doing **day shifts** on the surgical ward as normal.
Set up a **40-a-month** standing order into a savings pot.
Use the **AI helper** now and then to plan wound care revision.
feel: **Relieved** that the ward and her colleagues stay as they are.
A bit **flat**, because her real money worries don't change at all.
S0.quote: Nothing changing sounds lovely until you remember that nothing changing means the car loan, the 40-minute drive and the same short-staffed shifts.
fieldNote: Her job feels **secure**; the unease comes from the commute and a 600 clutch bill last winter.
She names the **ward clerk**, showing she notices who props up the ward.
She uses AI only **now and then**, for revision, and doesn't see it as a threat here.

steps.text: Keep working day shifts on the surgical ward
Set up a 40-a-month standing order into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels real. I can see the start of it already, with the new discharge software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI that writes discharge letters is great if it gives me more time at the bedside. But I'd also be saying the unions need to be at the table, because these tools always end up as an excuse to cut staff. I'd say both, probably in the same breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly fine, honestly. Hands-on surgical nursing isn't going anywhere fast. What worries me is Ines. My girlfriend helps seven-year-olds learn to read. If an app does that cheaper, our rent is suddenly my problem alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally apply for the wound care course at the university, the six-month one, because that's the bit of nursing a machine can't easily do. I'd do the hospital's training on the new AI note tools once a couple of people on the ward said they actually worked. And I'd go to the union meeting about the discharge software, which I usually skip because of the drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. Fine about my own job, a low hum of worry about Ines and the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you and Ines talked about her job and AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, after she saw a reading app at a training day. She laughed it off and said the kids would throw the tablets at the wall. I didn't push it, but I've thought about it on the drive more than once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If her hours did get cut, what changes at home first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan has to be paid, so it'd be food and her phone contract. We'd stop going out, which isn't much anyway. I might pick up extra bank shifts on weekends, which means seeing her even less.

say: I'd say AI writing **discharge letters** is welcome if it frees time at the bedside.
I'd insist the **unions** sit at the table so tools don't become an excuse for cuts.
think: My **hands-on** surgical work feels safe for a good while yet.
My girlfriend's **teaching assistant** job is the one I'd actually worry about.
do: Apply for the **six-month wound care course** at the university.
Do the **AI note training** once colleagues say the tools actually work.
Go to the **union meeting** about discharge software instead of skipping it.
feel: **Fine** about her own job but carrying a low hum of worry.
**Uneasy** about money if her girlfriend's school hours shrink.
S1.quote: My girlfriend helps seven-year-olds learn to read. If an app does that cheaper, our rent is suddenly my problem alone.
fieldNote: Her anxiety is about the **household**, not herself; her girlfriend's job is more exposed than hers.
She'd adopt AI tools only once **colleagues vouch** for them, true to her steady nature.
Weekend **bank shifts** are her fallback, at the cost of time with her partner.

steps.text: Apply for the six-month wound care course at the university
Do the AI note-writing training once colleagues vouch for it
Go to the union meeting about the discharge software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's really fast. Robots in 2031. Okay, give me a second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need strong unions and government stepping in, a proper safety net. I'd be telling people at work not to panic, because the hands-on stuff gives us a few years. Online I'd probably be angrier than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can still dress a wound in 2028, but my girlfriend's job at the primary school would be gone first, and we'd be living on one nurse's wage. Then by 2031 the robots start on my side too. The wound care course suddenly looks like it buys me three years, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the wound care course anyway, straight away, because three years of being the specialist is better than nothing. We'd sell the car and get a cheaper one outright, to kill the loan. I'd pick up two bank shifts a month. And I'd join whatever campaign the union runs for a guaranteed income for people pushed out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. And guilty, a bit, because I'd be the "safe" one in our house for a while and Ines wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots mean for your actual day on the ward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The charts, the obs, the drug checks would be done by the system by 2028, so I'd be doing pure hands-on care. Dressings, getting people up, holding someone's hand before theatre. That's honestly the bit I like, so there's a strange good side to it, until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ines's family help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her mum would, without being asked, which is lovely and also hard for me. I'd hate leaning on her again after the clutch. But if it's that or missing the rent, I'd swallow it.

say: I'd say we need **strong unions** and a proper government safety net.
I'd tell colleagues not to panic because **hands-on care** gives nurses a few more years.
think: Her girlfriend's **school job** goes first, leaving them on one nurse's wage.
The wound care course now buys **three years**, not a whole career.
do: Start the **wound care course** straight away despite the short horizon.
Sell the car and buy a **cheaper one outright** to clear the loan.
Pick up **two bank shifts** a month and join the union's income campaign.
feel: **Scared**, properly, about losing half the household income.
**Guilty** about being the safe one in the house while her girlfriend isn't.
S2.quote: I can still dress a wound in 2028, but my girlfriend's job at the primary school would be gone first, and we'd be living on one nurse's wage.
fieldNote: Her alarm comes from expecting a **household earner** to lose her job by 2028.
She sees a **good side** in pure hands-on care during the gap, until robots arrive.
Leaning on her girlfriend's **mother** again is the help she'd accept but resent.

steps.text: Start the wound care course straight away
Sell the car and buy a cheaper one outright
Accept help from her girlfriend's mother if rent can't be paid
Join the union's campaign for a guaranteed income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. 2031, and the robots around 2034. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them: training budgets, retraining for teaching assistants and admin staff, rules on robots in hospitals. That's the kind of thing I'd write to the council about. I'd sound calmer, but the message is the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to finish a wound care course and short enough that I'd skip the wedding party to pay for it. Ines and I have been talking about a small do next summer. I'd want us to have something in the bank first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the wound care course in the first year and then aim for a specialist post by 2028. I'd help Ines look at retraining, maybe as a speech therapy assistant, something with people. We'd put the wedding off to 2029 and put that 2,000 we'd saved into the emergency pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but in a planning way rather than a scared way. Five years means I can make a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did postponing the wedding feel like when you said it just now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad, honestly. My gran's been asking when it is, and she's 84. But Ines would agree, she's more careful than me about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, does using AI tools yourself start to matter more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. By year two or three I'd want to be the one on the ward who knows how the wound photo app works and when it's wrong. Not first, I'm never first, but not last.

say: I'd say five years is time for **training budgets** and rules on robots in hospitals.
I'd write to the **council** about retraining support for school and admin staff.
think: Five years lets me finish a **wound care course** before the change bites.
Paying for it might mean **skipping the wedding party** planned for next summer.
do: Finish the **wound care course** in year one and aim for a specialist post.
Help her girlfriend look at **retraining** as a speech therapy assistant.
Move the **2,000** wedding fund into the emergency pot and delay to 2029.
feel: **Worried** in a planning way rather than a scared way.
**Sad** about delaying the wedding while her 84-year-old gran waits.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to finish a wound care course and short enough that I'd skip the wedding party to pay for it.
fieldNote: The extra time turns fear into **lists**, but household income is still at risk.
Delaying the **wedding** is the real cost, sharpened by her elderly grandmother.
She wants to be **"not first, not last"** with AI tools, her steady nature in one line.

steps.text: Finish the wound care course and apply for a specialist post
Postpone the wedding to 2029 and move 2,000 into savings
Learn the wound photo app well enough to spot its mistakes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036, robots around 2039. I'd be 37 when the AGI part lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for the government to get this right, so there's no excuse. I'd be pushing for nurses to train the systems rather than be replaced by them. Calmly, at union meetings, not shouting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd stop being scared of the tools and start being the nurse who knows how to check them. I'd still be on lower pay in the meantime, though. AI doesn't fix the petrol bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wound care course first, then maybe a master's part-time later on, paid for by the hospital if I can get them to. Ines would have time to retrain properly, maybe a three-year degree. We'd have the wedding next summer as planned, small, and keep saving afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A little uneasy, because ten years always turns out shorter than you think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ines on the night you heard this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we've got a decade, which is longer than we've been together. Then I'd probably make her look at university courses with me over tea. She'd roll her eyes but she'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about ten years that makes you less likely to act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, actually. I'm the type who'd put it off. With two years I'd have no choice, with ten I'd keep saying "next year". I'd need Ines or someone at work to give me a push.

say: I'd say ten years gives government **no excuse** to get this wrong.
I'd argue nurses should **train the systems** rather than be replaced by them.
think: With ten years I'd become the nurse who **checks the tools**, not fears them.
The **petrol bill** and lower pay stay the same whatever AI does.
do: Do the **wound care course**, then push the hospital to fund a part-time master's.
Support her girlfriend through a **three-year degree** while there's time.
Hold the **small wedding** next summer as planned and keep saving afterwards.
feel: Mostly **okay**, with a decade to plan.
A little **uneasy**, because ten years always turns out shorter than expected.
S4.quote: With ten years, I'd stop being scared of the tools and start being the nurse who knows how to check them.
fieldNote: The decade is the only picture where she **keeps the wedding** on schedule.
She openly admits she'd **put things off** with too much time, a self-aware risk.
Her pay worries remain, but she now feels her **job and household** can adapt.

steps.text: Take the wound care course, then ask the hospital to fund a master's
Hold the small wedding next summer as planned
Help her girlfriend choose a university course this year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because of Ines. My job holds on a bit longer but hers doesn't, and we've got no cushion. What would help is proper retraining money for people like teaching assistants, paid while they study, and a hospital that pays for my course instead of making me use annual leave for it. The robots coming three years later doesn't feel like a reprieve. It feels like three years to work out what I'm for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how far people live from work. Nobody talks about the drive. If jobs move or shrink, those of us in villages with one bus a day get hit twice.

headlineQuote: The robots coming three years later doesn't feel like a reprieve. It feels like three years to work out what I'm for.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old surgical nurse** who drives 40 minutes each way to the regional hospital.
She loves **wound care** and keeps meaning to train in it properly.
Her biggest worry is her girlfriend Ines, a **teaching assistant** whose job looks more exposed than hers.
She moves from uneasy to **alarmed** in the two-year picture, then plans calmly with more time.
She adopts tools **once proven**, and admits a decade would tempt her to put things off.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her girlfriend's school job would go first with no savings to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** for teaching assistants and similar staff while they study.
The hospital **funding her course** instead of making her use annual leave.
